titleZh: Y Combinator 是如何起步的

segments.enMarkdown: Y Combinator's 7th birthday was March 11. As usual we were so busy we didn't notice till a few days after. I don't think we've ever managed to remember our birthday on our birthday.
segments.zhMarkdown: 3 月 11 日是 Y Combinator 的 7 周年纪念日。像往常一样，我们忙得不可开交，直到几天后才意识到。我想我们还从来没有在生日当天想起过自己的生日。

segments.enMarkdown: On March 11 2005, Jessica and I were walking home from dinner in Harvard Square. Jessica was working at an investment bank at the time, but she didn't like it much, so she had interviewed for a job as director of marketing at a Boston VC fund. The VC fund was doing what now seems a comically familiar thing for a VC fund to do: taking a long time to make up their mind. Meanwhile I had been telling Jessica all the things they should change about the VC business — essentially the ideas now underlying Y Combinator: investors should be making more, smaller investments, they should be funding hackers instead of suits, they should be willing to fund younger founders, etc.
segments.zhMarkdown: 2005年3月11日，我和杰西卡在哈佛广场吃完晚饭散步回家。杰西卡当时在一家投资银行工作，但她并不太喜欢，于是去波士顿的一家风投基金面试了市场总监的职位。这家风投基金正做着一件如今看来风投圈司空见惯、甚至有些滑稽的事：迟迟拿不定主意。与此同时，我一直在跟杰西卡念叨风投行业应该做出的种种改变——这些想法本质上正是如今 Y Combinator 的基石：投资人应该做更多笔、金额更小的投资；应该资助黑客而不是穿西装的人；应该愿意资助更年轻的创始人，诸如此类。

segments.enMarkdown:
At the time I had been thinking about doing some angel investing. I had just given a talk to the undergraduate computer club at Harvard about [how to start a
startup](https://paulgraham.com/start.html), and it hit me afterward that although I had always meant to do angel investing, 7 years had now passed since I got enough money to do it, and I still hadn't started. I had also been thinking about ways to work with Robert Morris and Trevor Blackwell again. A few hours before I had sent them an email trying to figure out what we could do together.
segments.zhMarkdown: 那时候我一直在考虑做点天使投资。我刚给哈佛大学的本科生电脑社团做了一场关于[如何创业](https://paulgraham.com/start.html)的演讲。演讲结束后我突然意识到，虽然我一直打算做天使投资，但自从我赚到足够的钱到现在已经过去了 7 年，我却迟迟没有动手。同时，我也在想办法能和 Robert Morris 以及 Trevor Blackwell 再次合作。几个小时前，我还给他们发了封邮件，想探讨一下我们能一起做点什么。

segments.enMarkdown: Between Harvard Square and my house the idea gelled. We'd start our own investment firm and Jessica could work for that instead. As we turned onto Walker Street we decided to do it. I agreed to put $100k into the new fund and Jessica agreed to quit her job to work for it. Over the next couple days I recruited Robert and Trevor, who put in another $50k each. So YC started with $200k.
segments.zhMarkdown: 在哈佛广场到我家的路上，这个想法成型了。我们要创办自己的投资公司，这样 Jessica 就可以来这里工作了。当我们拐进沃克街（Walker Street）时，我们决定就这么干。我同意往新基金里投入 10 万美元，Jessica 也同意辞职来这里工作。接下来的几天里，我拉上了 Robert 和 Trevor，他们各投了 5 万美元。所以，YC 是带着 20 万美元起步的。

segments.enMarkdown: Jessica was so happy to be able to quit her job and start her own company that I took her [picture](https://web.archive.org/web/20170609055553/http://www.ycombinator.com/yc05.html) when we got home.
segments.zhMarkdown: Jessica 终于能辞去工作并开始创办自己的公司，她太高兴了，以至于我们一回到家，我就给她拍了张[照片](https://web.archive.org/web/20170609055553/http://www.ycombinator.com/yc05.html)。

segments.enMarkdown: The company wasn't called Y Combinator yet. At first we called it Cambridge Seed. But that name never saw the light of day, because by the time we announced it a few days later, we'd changed the name to Y Combinator. We realized early on that what we were doing could be national in scope and we didn't want a name that tied us to one place.
segments.zhMarkdown: 这家公司当时还不叫 Y Combinator。起初我们称它为 Cambridge Seed（剑桥种子基金）。但这个名字从未真正公开过，因为几天后我们宣布成立时，已经把名字改成了 Y Combinator。我们很早就意识到，我们所做的事情可能是全国性的，我们不想用一个把我们限制在某个地方的名字。

segments.enMarkdown: Initially we only had part of the idea. We were going to do seed funding with standardized terms. Before YC, seed funding was very haphazard. You'd get that first $10k from your friend's rich uncle. The deal terms were often a disaster; often neither the investor nor the founders nor the lawyer knew what the documents should look like. Facebook's early history as a Florida LLC shows how random things could be in those days. We were going to be something there had not been before: a standard source of seed funding.
segments.zhMarkdown: 起初，我们只构想出了这个想法的一部分。我们打算用标准化的条款来进行种子轮融资。在 YC 出现之前，种子轮融资非常混乱。你的第一笔 1 万美元可能来自你朋友的有钱叔叔。交易条款往往是一场灾难；投资人、创始人和律师通常都不知道这些文件应该长什么样。Facebook 早期在佛罗里达州注册为有限责任公司（LLC）的经历，就表明了那个时候的事情有多么随机。我们要做的是一个前所未有的东西：一个标准化的种子基金来源。

segments.enMarkdown: We modelled YC on the seed funding we ourselves had taken when we started Viaweb. We started Viaweb with $10k we got from our friend [Julian Weber](https://paulgraham.com/julian.html), the husband of Idelle Weber, whose painting class I took as a grad student at Harvard. Julian knew about business, but you would not describe him as a suit. Among other things he'd been president of the *National Lampoon*. He was also a lawyer, and got all our paperwork set up properly. In return for $10k, getting us set up as a company, teaching us what business was about, and remaining calm in times of crisis, Julian got 10% of Viaweb. I remember thinking once what a good deal Julian got. And then a second later I realized that without Julian, Viaweb would never have made it. So even though it was a good deal for him, it was a good deal for us too. That's why I knew there was room for something like Y Combinator.
segments.zhMarkdown: 我们是以自己创办 Viaweb 时获得的种子投资为雏形来设计 YC 的。我们创办 Viaweb 时，启动资金是来自朋友 [Julian Weber](https://paulgraham.com/julian.html) 的一万美元。他是艾德尔·韦伯（Idelle Weber）的丈夫，我在哈佛读研究生时上过她的绘画课。朱利安懂商业，但你绝不会觉得他是个穿西装的刻板商务人士。除其他成就外，他还当过 *National Lampoon* 的社长。他也是一名律师，帮我们把所有法律手续都办得妥妥当当。作为提供一万美元、帮我们完成公司注册、教我们理解商业运作，以及在危机时刻保持冷静的回报，朱利安拿到了 Viaweb 10% 的股份。我记得自己曾一度觉得朱利安做了一笔多么划算的买卖。但紧接着我就意识到，如果没有朱利安，Viaweb 根本不可能做成。所以，这对他来说固然很划算，对我们而言也同样如此。正因如此，我知道市场上一定有容纳 Y Combinator 这种机构的空间。

segments.enMarkdown: Initially we didn't have what turned out to be the most important idea: funding startups synchronously, instead of asynchronously as it had always been done before. Or rather we had the idea, but we didn't realize its significance. We decided very early that the first thing we'd do would be to fund a bunch of startups over the coming summer. But we didn't realize initially that this would be the way we'd do all our investing. The reason we began by funding a bunch of startups at once was not that we thought it would be a better way to fund startups, but simply because we wanted to learn how to be angel investors, and a summer program for undergrads seemed the fastest way to do it. No one takes summer jobs that seriously. The opportunity cost for a bunch of undergrads to spend a summer working on startups was low enough that we wouldn't feel guilty encouraging them to do it.
segments.zhMarkdown: 起初，我们并没有想到那个后来被证明是最重要的创意：同时（批量同步地）资助创业公司，而不是像以前那样零散（异步地）资助。或者更准确地说，我们有这个想法，但没有意识到它的重要性。我们很早就决定，我们要做的第一件事就是在即将到来的夏天资助一批创业公司。但我们起初并没有意识到，这将成为我们以后所有投资的方式。我们之所以一开始就一次性资助一批创业公司，并不是因为我们觉得这是一种更好的投资方式，而仅仅是因为我们想学习如何做天使投资人，而针对本科生的暑期项目似乎是实现这一目标最快的方式。没有人会把暑期工看得太重。对一群本科生来说，花一个暑假去创业的机会成本足够低，我们鼓励他们去尝试也不会觉得有负罪感。

segments.enMarkdown: We knew students would already be making plans for the summer, so we did what we're always telling startups to do: we launched fast. Here are the initial [announcement](https://paulgraham.com/summerfounder.html) and [description](https://web.archive.org/web/20170609055553/http://ycombinator.com/old/sfp.html) of what was at the time called the Summer Founders Program.
segments.zhMarkdown: 我们知道学生们当时已经在制定暑期计划了，所以我们做了我们总是叮嘱创业公司要做的事：快速发布。这是当时被称为“暑期创始人计划”（Summer Founders Program）的最初[公告](https://paulgraham.com/summerfounder.html)和[介绍](https://web.archive.org/web/20170609055553/http://ycombinator.com/old/sfp.html)。

segments.enMarkdown: We got lucky in that the length and structure of a summer program turns out to be perfect for what we do. The structure of the YC cycle is still almost identical to what it was that first summer.
segments.zhMarkdown: 我们很幸运，暑期项目的时长和结构被证明完美契合我们所做的事情。如今 YC 运营周期的结构，依然与那个首个夏天的模式几乎完全一致。

segments.enMarkdown: We also got lucky in who the first batch of founders were. We never expected to make any money from that first batch. We thought of the money we were investing as a combination of an educational expense and a charitable donation. But the founders in the first batch turned out to be surprisingly good. And great people too. We're still friends with a lot of them today.
segments.zhMarkdown: 我们在第一批创始人的选择上也极为幸运。我们从未指望能从第一批项目中赚到钱。我们把投资的钱看作是教育支出和慈善捐款的结合。但第一批创始人却出乎意料地优秀。而且他们人也非常好。直到今天，我们和他们中的许多人依然是朋友。

segments.enMarkdown: It's hard for people to realize now how inconsequential YC seemed at the time. I can't blame people who didn't take us seriously, because we ourselves didn't take that first summer program seriously in the very beginning. But as the summer progressed we were increasingly impressed by how well the startups were doing. Other people started to be impressed too. Jessica and I invented a term, "the Y Combinator effect," to describe the moment when the realization hit someone that YC was not totally lame. When people came to YC to speak at the dinners that first summer, they came in the spirit of someone coming to address a Boy Scout troop. By the time they left the building they were all saying some variant of "Wow, these companies might actually succeed."
segments.zhMarkdown: 现在的人很难想象，当时的 YC 看起来是多么微不足道。我不能怪那些不把我们当回事的人，因为我们自己一开始也没把那个暑期项目太当回事。但随着夏天的推进，创业公司表现出来的优异成绩让我们越来越感到震惊。其他人也开始刮目相看。我和 Jessica 发明了一个词，叫“Y Combinator 效应”，用来形容别人突然意识到 YC 没那么逊的那个瞬间。那个夏天，当人们来 YC 的晚餐会上做演讲时，他们来的时候抱着的态度就像是在给童子军训话。而当他们离开大楼时，所有人都在说类似的话：“哇，这些公司可能真的会成功。”

segments.enMarkdown: Now YC is well enough known that people are no longer surprised when the companies we fund are legit, but it took a while for reputation to catch up with reality. That's one of the reasons we especially like funding ideas that might be dismissed as "toys" — because YC itself was dismissed as one initially.
segments.zhMarkdown: 如今 YC 的名气已经足够大，当我们投资的公司名副其实、大获成功时，人们已不再感到惊讶，但声誉赶上现实确实经历了一段时间。这也是我们格外喜欢资助那些可能被斥为“玩具”的创意的理由之一——因为 YC 本身在一开始也曾被人当成玩具而不屑一顾。

segments.enMarkdown: When we saw how well it worked to fund companies synchronously, we decided we'd keep doing that. We'd fund two batches of startups a year.
segments.zhMarkdown: 当我们看到同步资助公司的效果如此之好时，我们决定继续做下去。我们每年将资助两批创业公司。

segments.enMarkdown: We funded the second batch in Silicon Valley. That was a last minute decision. In retrospect I think what pushed me over the edge was going to Foo Camp that fall. The density of startup people in the Bay Area was so much greater than in Boston, and the weather was so nice. I remembered that from living there in the 90s. Plus I didn't want someone else to copy us and describe it as the Y Combinator of Silicon Valley. I wanted YC to be the Y Combinator of Silicon Valley. So doing the winter batch in California seemed like one of those rare cases where the self-indulgent choice and the ambitious one were the same.
segments.zhMarkdown: 我们在硅谷资助了第二批项目。那是一个在最后一刻做出的决定。回想起来，我认为推动我做出这一决定的，是那年秋天去参加了 Foo Camp。湾区创业者的密度比波士顿大得多，而且天气也太好了。这让我想起了 90 年代在那里生活的感觉。此外，我不想让别人抄袭我们，并自称为“硅谷的 Y Combinator”。我希望 YC 自己就是硅谷的 Y Combinator。所以，在加州做冬季班，似乎是极少数既满足个人偏好又符合雄心壮志的完美结合。

segments.enMarkdown: If we'd had enough time to do what we wanted, Y Combinator would have been in Berkeley. That was our favorite part of the Bay Area. But we didn't have time to get a building in Berkeley. We didn't have time to get our own building anywhere. The only way to get enough space in time was to convince Trevor to let us take over part of his (as it then seemed) giant building in Mountain View. Yet again we lucked out, because Mountain View turned out to be the ideal place to put something like YC. But even then we barely made it. The first dinner in California, we had to warn all the founders not to touch the walls, because the paint was still wet.
segments.zhMarkdown: 如果我们有足够的时间来做想做的事，Y Combinator 本该设在伯克利。那是我们在湾区最喜欢的地方。但我们没有时间在伯克利弄到一栋楼。我们甚至没时间在任何地方弄到一栋属于自己的楼。在时间紧迫的情况下，获得足够空间的唯一办法，就是说服 Trevor 让我们接管他在山景城那栋（在当时看来）巨大的大楼的一部分。我们再次走运了，因为事实证明，山景城是放置 YC 这种机构的理想地点。但即便如此，我们也差点没赶上。在加州的第一次晚餐会上，我们不得不警告所有的创始人不要碰墙壁，因为油漆还没干。
